Helping Your Child Believe in Themselves

Every child develops a sense of who they are through their experiences, relationships and the way people respond to them.

A child may begin to question themselves when they experience repeated difficulties, criticism, comparison, friendship problems, bullying, challenges at school or situations where they feel they are not good enough.

You may notice your child becoming hesitant to try new things, giving up quickly, comparing themselves with other children, avoiding challenges, or becoming very upset when they make mistakes.

Perhaps they are saying things like:

"I'm not good at this."

"I can't do it."

"Everyone else is better than me."

"I'm not good enough."

When these beliefs begin to affect how a child sees themselves and participates in everyday life, additional support may be helpful.

Your child does not need to be struggling significantly before you seek guidance.

With the right support, children can develop a stronger sense of self, recognise their strengths, learn to work through challenges and build confidence through their own experiences.

Understanding Self-Esteem

What Is Self-Esteem?

Self-esteem is the way a child views themselves, including how they see their abilities, strengths and sense of self-worth.

It is not simply about being confident or believing that you are good at everything.

Healthy self-esteem can involve being able to recognise:

  • "I have strengths."
  • "I can learn new things."
  • "I can make mistakes and try again."
  • "I can ask for help when I need it."
  • "I have things that I can contribute."
  • "I am still worthwhile when something doesn't go as planned."

Children develop these beliefs through everyday experiences.

When children have opportunities to make choices, try things for themselves, solve problems and experience their own progress, they can begin to develop a stronger sense of capability and agency.

Could This Be What Your Child Is Experiencing?

When Low Self-Esteem Starts Showing Up in Everyday Life

Children do not always say, "I have low self-esteem."

Instead, it may appear through their behaviour, emotions, relationships or willingness to participate.

You may notice that your child:

  • frequently says they are "bad" at things
  • gives up quickly when something becomes difficult
  • avoids trying new activities because they are afraid of getting it wrong
  • becomes very upset by mistakes
  • compares themselves with other children
  • finds it difficult to accept compliments
  • focuses heavily on what they cannot do
  • seems reluctant to participate in class or group activities
  • avoids social situations because they are worried about what others think
  • becomes unusually quiet or withdrawn
  • relies heavily on adults to make decisions for them
  • seeks frequent reassurance about whether they are doing something correctly
  • becomes very self-critical
  • has difficulty recognising their own strengths
  • appears less willing to take healthy risks or try unfamiliar activities

Some children may also become frustrated, defensive or upset when they feel they are not succeeding.

Low self-esteem can look different from child to child.

The important consideration is how these patterns are affecting your child's confidence, relationships, participation and everyday wellbeing.

You May Be Looking for Support Because...

Perhaps:

  • your child is constantly comparing themselves with other children
  • they are afraid of making mistakes
  • they avoid activities they used to enjoy
  • they become upset when they do not succeed immediately
  • they believe they are "not good enough"
  • they have difficulty making friends or joining activities
  • they are reluctant to speak up or share their ideas
  • school challenges are affecting their confidence
  • bullying or exclusion has affected how they see themselves
  • your child has experienced a significant change or difficult situation
  • you are constantly reassuring them, but they continue to doubt themselves
  • you can see their strengths, but they struggle to see them themselves
  • you are unsure how to encourage confidence without putting additional pressure on them

You do not need to wait until low self-esteem is affecting every part of your child's life.

A conversation with an appropriately qualified practitioner can help you understand what may be contributing to your child's difficulties and what type of support may be appropriate.

What Can Affect a Child's Self-Esteem?

Self-Esteem Develops Through Experiences

There is rarely one single reason why a child develops low self-esteem.

A child's sense of self can be influenced by their relationships, environment, experiences and opportunities to develop their skills and independence.

Comparison

Children naturally notice how they compare with others.

Repeated comparison with siblings, classmates, teammates or peers can affect how a child views their own abilities.

Bullying and Social Exclusion

Being bullied, excluded or feeling that they do not belong can negatively affect a child's sense of self-worth.

Difficult Experiences

Repeated experiences of failure, criticism or feeling unable to meet expectations may lead a child to develop negative beliefs about themselves.

Too Much Help

Adults naturally want to help children.

However, when adults regularly take over tasks that children could gradually learn to do themselves, children may have fewer opportunities to experience their own capability and accomplishment.

Limited Opportunities to Make Choices

Age-appropriate choices can help children develop a sense of control and confidence in their ability to make decisions.

Relationships and Belonging

Children's relationships with parents, caregivers, siblings, friends and teachers can contribute to how they understand themselves and their place in the world.

Challenges at School or in Activities

Academic, sporting, social or other difficulties can affect confidence, particularly when a child begins to believe that struggling means they are incapable.

A child's difficulties do not define their worth.

Support can help children separate who they are from what they find difficult.

When "I Can't" Becomes "I'll Try"

Building Confidence Through Small Experiences

Confidence does not have to come before a child tries something difficult.

Often, confidence develops because a child has opportunities to try, practise, make mistakes, receive support and experience progress.

For one child, this might mean:

  • joining a new activity
  • speaking up in class
  • trying a task they previously avoided
  • making a new friend
  • learning a new skill
  • making an age-appropriate decision
  • solving a problem independently
  • recovering after making a mistake

The goal is not to make every experience easy.

It is to help your child discover, "I can handle difficult things."

What Could Change with the Right Support?

Helping Your Child Develop a Stronger Sense of Self

Therapy is not about convincing a child that they are perfect or telling them that they should always feel confident.

It can help them develop a more balanced and compassionate understanding of themselves.

With appropriate support, a child may learn to:

  • recognise their strengths
  • understand and express their emotions
  • identify unhelpful self-critical thoughts
  • challenge "I can't" thinking
  • recognise that skills develop through practice
  • cope with mistakes and setbacks
  • develop problem-solving skills
  • make age-appropriate decisions
  • communicate their needs
  • accept appropriate support
  • recognise their own progress
  • try new experiences
  • develop resilience when things do not go as planned

The goal is not a child who never doubts themselves.

It is helping them develop the confidence to keep learning, growing and trying even when things feel difficult.

For Parents

Your Response Can Help Shape Their Confidence

Parents and caregivers have an important role in helping children develop self-esteem.

Children learn from how adults respond when they succeed, struggle, make mistakes and face challenges.

Praise Effort and Progress

Rather than focusing only on whether your child succeeded, notice the effort, persistence and problem-solving they used.

For example:

"I noticed you kept trying even when that was difficult."

Specific praise can help children understand what they are doing well.

Encourage Independence

Allow your child to do age-appropriate tasks for themselves, even when it would be quicker for you to do them.

Small opportunities to take responsibility can help children experience their own capability.

Give Appropriate Choices

Offer manageable choices and allow your child to experience the consequences of reasonable decisions.

Listen to Their Ideas

Show your child that their thoughts and opinions matter.

Avoid Constant Comparison

Help your child recognise that people have different strengths, interests and areas for development.

Encourage Rather Than Rescue

When something is difficult, provide support without immediately taking over.

Sometimes the most helpful message is:

"Let's work out what you could try."

Notice Their Strengths

Help your child recognise qualities beyond academic or performance achievements, such as kindness, persistence, creativity, curiosity, humour, courage or willingness to help others.

Create a Sense of Belonging

Positive relationships with family, friends and other supportive adults can help children develop a stronger sense of self and feel valued.

Building Self-Esteem at Home

Small Everyday Experiences Can Make a Difference

Self-esteem is not built through one conversation.

It develops through repeated experiences of being supported, encouraged, listened to and given opportunities to grow.

You can help your child by:

  • noticing their effort
  • celebrating progress
  • encouraging them to try again after setbacks
  • allowing them to solve age-appropriate problems
  • giving them opportunities to make choices
  • encouraging healthy friendships
  • listening to their ideas
  • helping them identify their strengths
  • modelling respectful self-talk
  • reminding them that mistakes are part of learning
  • creating opportunities for them to contribute at home
  • encouraging activities that allow them to develop skills and interests

Small successes can become building blocks for greater confidence.

Goals, Dreams and Personal Growth

Helping Your Child Believe in What They Can Become

Children benefit from having goals that are meaningful to them.

Rather than deciding what your child should achieve, encourage them to think about what they enjoy, what they would like to learn and what they would like to work towards.

Large goals can be broken into smaller, achievable steps.

For example:

Big goal:

"I want to learn how to play soccer."

Small steps:

  • practise one skill
  • attend training
  • ask a coach for help
  • practise regularly
  • notice progress over time

Breaking larger goals into manageable steps can help children experience progress and develop confidence in their ability to learn.

The aim is not achievement for approval.

It is helping your child discover what matters to them and experience the satisfaction of making progress.

When Should You Seek Professional Support?

You Don't Have to Wait Until Confidence Has Disappeared

It may be helpful to seek professional guidance when low self-esteem:

  • persists over time
  • is significantly affecting your child's daily life
  • prevents them from trying activities
  • affects friendships or participation
  • is associated with significant anxiety or low mood
  • causes persistent negative self-talk
  • leads to increasing withdrawal
  • affects school participation
  • makes everyday challenges particularly difficult
  • is causing significant distress for your child or family

Low self-esteem can sometimes occur alongside anxiety or depression, so it is important to consider the child's broader emotional wellbeing rather than looking at self-esteem in isolation. If you are unsure whether your child needs therapy, you can still reach out for guidance. A qualified practitioner can help assess your child's individual circumstances and determine whether psychological support may be beneficial.

What Could Therapy Look Like?

Individualised Support for Your Child

There is no single approach to building self-esteem.

Therapy should be appropriate to your child's age, developmental stage, individual needs and circumstances.

Depending on the child, therapy may involve:

Understanding Self-Talk

Helping children recognise overly negative or self-critical thoughts and develop more balanced ways of thinking about themselves.

Strengths-Based Work

Helping children identify their abilities, interests, values and personal qualities.

Emotional Regulation

Teaching age-appropriate strategies for understanding and managing difficult emotions.

Problem-Solving Skills

Helping children approach challenges as problems they can work through rather than evidence that they are incapable.

Confidence Through Practice

Supporting children to take manageable steps towards activities or situations they have been avoiding.

Building Independence

Encouraging age-appropriate decision-making and opportunities for children to experience their own capability.

Parent Guidance

Parents may be involved in therapy to learn practical ways to reinforce their child's progress at home.

Social and Relationship Support

Where appropriate, therapy may explore friendship difficulties, belonging, communication and other experiences affecting the child's sense of self.

The right approach will depend on your child's individual needs and should be determined by a suitably qualified practitioner.

You Don't Need to Know Where to Start

Finding the Right Support for Your Child

It can be difficult to know whether your child needs therapy, parent guidance, support with a particular difficulty, or simply some additional encouragement.

You don't need to diagnose your child before contacting us.

You can tell us what you have been noticing, what seems difficult for your child and how these concerns are affecting everyday life.

Our team can help gather the relevant information and guide you towards an appropriate practitioner or support pathway based on your child's needs.

Whether your child is struggling with confidence, negative self-talk, fear of failure, social difficulties, comparison, withdrawal, or difficulty trying new things, we can help you explore the next step.

Why Families Choose MBP

Clinically Informed Support, With Children and Families at the Centre

Michelle Barratt Psychology & Administrative Services (MBP) provides a professional and supportive entry point for families seeking psychological and allied health care.

Our role is to make accessing support clearer and more manageable while helping families connect with practitioners whose experience aligns with their child's needs.

Clinically Informed Intake

Our intake process helps us understand your concerns and identify an appropriate support pathway for your child.

Child-Focused Matching

We help families identify practitioners who work with children and whose experience is relevant to the concerns described.

Family Support

We assist parents and caregivers with referrals, appointments, intake requirements and administrative processes.

Age-Appropriate Care

Children have different developmental needs at different ages. We help families connect with practitioners whose experience is appropriate to their child's stage of development.

Coordinated Support

Where appropriate and with the necessary consent, practitioners may liaise with schools, GPs and other professionals involved in your child's care.

Flexible Access

In-person appointments are available across Brisbane, with telehealth options available Australia-wide where clinically appropriate and offered by the practitioner.

Start with a Conversation

Your Child Can Learn to Believe in Themselves

Maybe your child has started saying they are not good enough.

Maybe they are avoiding things they once enjoyed, becoming afraid of making mistakes, comparing themselves with other children, or finding it difficult to recognise their own strengths. Or perhaps you simply feel that your child does not see themselves in the positive way that you see them.

You don't need to have all the answers before reaching out.

Start by telling us a little about what you have been noticing and what you would like support with.

We'll help you understand the next steps and explore an appropriate pathway for your child. Contact Michelle Barratt Psychology to learn more about support for your child's self-esteem and confidence.
